Scientists still haven’t cracked how to turn water into wine—but they might have figured out how to turn beer into clean water. From the literal ashes of breweries’ by-products, researchers made a charcoal-like substance that clings to bacteria, and they are using it to test a new way of filtering water.

In a recent study, scientists heated up a common waste product from beer making called spent malt rootlets, which are little sprouts that grow from barley during the malting process, to produce biochar, a porous material created from burned organic matter. They found that when they mixed this substance with sand and sent water through it, the biochar was able to remove around five times as much Escherichia coli bacteria as a filtration system that used only sand.

Sending water through sand filtered bacteria like a colander: by physically stopping microbes from moving through. But when the team used a sand mix that was 10 percent biochar, the biochar actively glommed on to slow microbes’ passage.

Groundwater is constantly moving through soil. There it can become contaminated with agricultural waste or fecal matter—potentially infecting any humans who drink it. Adding biochar to certain soils could offer a public health solution and “a sustainable approach for water remediation and the protection of groundwater,” says Ioannis Manariotis, senior author on the study and an environmental engineer at the University of Patras in Greece.

Manariotis and his team have also tested whether waste from olive oil and coffee production can have similar water-purifying effects. Now that the researchers have found the beer by-product can filter out bacteria in laboratory conditions, he says, they plan to test its efficacy under more unpredictable real-life conditions. The results were published in the journal Biochar.

Using brewery waste for water filtration in this way is a “proof of concept,” says Alcina Johnson Sudagar, an independent chemistry researcher who studies other beer-making by-products and was not involved in the study. But the repurposing of by-products from this industry for other applications is already common, she says. Leftover brewery grain is frequently used to make animal feed, and other research suggests beer-making by-products can be used for everything from sunscreen to electricity. The brewing process can have up to 11 steps, and each step produces organic waste materials with different chemical makeups—potentially ideal for different uses.

Sudagar says she hopes Manariotis and his team continue to study biochar. Her most pressing question is whether the material can be used more than once for filtration. If it can trap bacteria only once, it quickly becomes waste again, negating its value as a consistent filtration system or sustainable brewery by-product.

As the global beer industry grows, these new and innovative ways of using the by-products are crucial to sustainability, Sudagar adds. “It’s important to continue because the waste produced will keep increasing, and you would need different applications,” she says. “You cannot just send it to one place and say that we are done with it.”

Scientists are continuing to look for ways to replace sugar in our diets. As great as it makes food taste, we know it's not great for our health, and questions have been raised over the impacts of artificial sweeteners too.
According to a new study published in Clinical Nutrition ESPEN, a protein called brazzein could be the answer.
Originally found in a West African fruit and now mostly made by engineered fungi, it's processed naturally and easily by the body and is up to 2,000 times sweeter than sugar, weight for weight.

Researchers from the Federal Research Center of Nutrition, Biotechnology and Food Safety in Russia ran tests with 101 adults diagnosed with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition often accompanied by obesity and diabetes, where fat builds up in the liver.
The study, a randomized controlled double-blind crossover trial, focused on ice cream, one of the most tempting types of sugary foods.

Each participant consumed a standard 100-gram (3.5-ounce) serving of vanilla ice cream on three separate days: one using sugar, one sweetened with brazzein, and one with brazzein and the dietary fiber inulin.

What stood out from the data was that post-meal rises in blood sugar were significantly cut by both brazzein and brazzein with inulin. The spikes were about half as large as with sugar-sweetened ice cream in both cases.
The sugar-free recipes also differed in other ingredients, so the researchers caution that they can't attribute the effect to brazzein alone.

"From a clinical nutrition perspective, the present findings indicate that the tested sucrose-free brazzein-containing formulations may warrant further investigation as potential sugar-substitution options for patients with MASLD, including those with type 2 diabetes," writes the team in their published paper.
The reductions in blood sugar spikes were actually more noticeable in the participants with type 2 diabetes, although still substantial in those without, while no serious side effects were reported.

It backs up previous research in mice suggesting that brazzein could work as a sugar substitute that keeps the sweetness without the downsides, and lays the foundation for studies that follow participants (and their blood sugar) across a longer time frame.

"The magnitude and timing of the observed effects support future studies of brazzein-sweetened foods," write the researchers, calling for longer studies that swap sugar for brazzein across a range of commonly eaten foods.

As a protein, brazzein is tough, withstanding temperatures up to 80 °C (176 °F) and a wide range of acidity levels, which means it could potentially be added to multiple foods – including frozen desserts.

However, as the researchers point out, sugar doesn't just add sweetness – in ice cream, it provides bulk and viscosity, for example. The study shows that other 'filler' ingredients alongside brazzein can work to make something very similar to the real thing.
An approach like this is also likely to have more impact than asking people to cut out sugar from their diets, as it means sweet treats aren't off the menu.

"Sugar-sweetened foods and beverages, including popular items such as ice cream, desserts, and confectioneries, are deeply embedded in dietary patterns worldwide and continue to grow," write the researchers.
"Extensive restriction of these products in the diet is often unrealistic and may lead to poor adherence to dietary recommendations."

There's still a lot of research to be carried out, but we could eventually see brazzein used in place of sugar in foods suitable for those with diabetes or a condition like MASLD, or who are trying to cut down on sugar in general.

What we don't have here is any indication of how brazzein-sweetened foods might affect liver fat, diabetes, blood pressure, or other related conditions over months or years. What's more, the participants in this study represented a narrow slice of the population – all with MASLD, and many diagnosed as obese.
We know that multiple factors can affect blood sugar, from who you're eating with to how you're eating. These factors can all be scrutinized in future research.

"Longer-term studies are needed to determine whether repeated substitution of sucrose-containing desserts with brazzein-sweetened alternatives translates into sustained metabolic, hepatic, microbiome, or behavioral benefits," write the researchers.
The research has been published in Clinical Nutrition ESPEN.
We Homo sapiens are pretty damn proud of our tool-making prowess.
From smartphones to the humble-yet-mighty wheel, our ability to craft objects to help us attain our goals is something that we've often thought defines us as a species.
But tens of thousands of years ago, Homo sapiens were not the only humans with a wide arsenal of tools.
In a recent dig at a significant Neanderthal site in Barcelona, Abric Romaní, archaeologists have unearthed a massive cache of wood imprints, several of which appear to be tools.
The findings, recently published in Science Advances, suggest our extinct Paleolithic relatives were actually skilled and prolific woodworkers.
Of the 597 wood imprints the team discovered, 13 are clearly modified tools and other domestic objects.
One of the most exciting objects identified was a wooden club, which seems to have been deliberately shaped for whacking stuff.
It's reminiscent of the classic 'caveman' costume prop, but archaeologists have never actually seen anything like it in the prehistoric record.

"To date, only one possible example has been reported from Kalambo Falls (Zambia), dated to ∼400 kyr," writes Palmira Saladié and a team of researchers based at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES).

"Consequently, assessing the precise function, use intensity, or behavioral context of such implements, particularly in relation to Neanderthal occupations at Abric Romaní, remains challenging given the limited comparative record and the functional variability documented among recent hunter-gatherers."
The team also found structural poles that may have been used for shelter; a tripod; some pointed wood objects that may be digging sticks; and two spears.
They believe four charred bark objects may have been used as trays or containers for food.
It's not the first evidence that Neanderthals may have made tools with wood, but it's possibly the most detailed and extensive collection of specimens.
In 1995, wooden weapons were found in Germany that dated back to 300,000 years ago, and in 2018, a paper described 171,000-year-old wooden tools found in Tuscany, Italy.
Another pair of artifacts found in Greece may also be Neanderthal – though in all these cases, it's more of an archaeologist's best guess as to who the craftsperson really was.
Wood tools are much less likely to be preserved than those made from stone, for instance, because of their organic quality: wood easily decays.

But at Abric Romaní, the imprints of wooden artifacts are preserved across layers of limestone. Even though the wood is long gone, calcium carbonate built up around the wood before it rotted away. This mineral cast left a negative imprint of the tool that survived the millennia.
In some cases, these imprints are so clear that the researchers can see details down to the cellular level, which is how they know they're looking at traces of wood.
"Wood technology likely played a key role in human evolution, yet it remains poorly documented because organic materials rarely preserve in archaeological contexts," Saladié and team note.

"The Abric Romaní assemblage highlights the importance of wood within Neanderthal technological systems and provides previously unknown insights into the role of organic materials in Middle Paleolithic societies."
The research has been published in Science Advances.

There's another notable first in the field of quantum physics to report on, and it's all to do with electron spin: the tiny, built-in magnetism of these particles, as if each one is carrying a microscopic compass needle.
Previously, the force of these spins has only proved enough to nudge individual atoms in one direction or another. Now though, researchers have managed to shift something much, much bigger.

A team from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) in Japan has published a new study in Science Advances that details how a centimeter-sized object can be nudged by these quantum forces.

It's an important step forward for science at the boundary of the quantum (very small scales) and the classical (everything else). Crucially, the experiment deals with an object big enough to be subject to gravity – a fundamental force that hasn't always sat well with the theories of quantum physics.
"There have been many efforts to test whether quantum mechanics holds for anything larger than a few tens of nanometers, so far without success," says theoretical physicist Jason Twamley.

"Now, we have observed a classical mechanical response to a quantum force on an object that is eight to nine orders of magnitude more massive than the current state-of-the-art spin-mechanical experiments."

The researchers combined several clever experimental design choices to get their results, starting with the centimeter-sized object: a graphite plate, placed above a checkerboard of magnets levitating it.

Hanging from the plate was a 3-millimeter diamond with special atomic defects known as nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers. These defects give the diamond electrons with controllable spins, which were then manipulated by laser light. Another magnet was then used to turn those spins into movement.
The whole assembly weighed around 128 milligrams (so just a few grains of rice), and was pushed by about 100 nanometers – roughly a thousandth of a human hair. It's not much, but it's enough.
"NV diamonds are well understood and easy to control," says physicist Daehee Kim.

"That, and the fact that NV centers have some of the longest known coherence times, allowing them to maintain quantum superposition at room temperature much longer than other systems, makes them particularly attractive for generating macroscopic superposition of the motion or object in future research."

When it comes to reconciling the massive (something like gravity's effect on a planet) with the subatomic and the quantum, scientists often try and start small and then work their way up. Here the study team took the opposite approach: their setup wasn't planet-sized, but was very large-scale in quantum terms.
"We're in the opposite camp – going from large to small," says physicist Anshuman Nayak.

"Just as diamagnetic levitation can lift maglev trains, it can also be used to levitate centimeter-wide objects holding diamonds, where the effect of gravity can be extremely strong, but quantum effects have not been observed."

As is often the case with quantum research, for those of us who aren't physicists it can seem rather esoteric and distant, but reaching milestones like this will help us answer some of the most profound questions about the Universe – including whether or not gravity follows quantum rules.

It's worth bearing in mind that the movement here was classical – it was the quantum effect that triggered the movement that's important. Further down the line, the researchers hope their approach can help in putting larger objects in quantum states, like superposition, where it effectively occupies two states at once.

"We've shown a large classical response from a small quantum effect," says Twamley. "It's no longer a question of whether such technology is possible, but of how we can refine experimental conditions to achieve quantum superposition within the regime of Einstein's general relativity."
"We're pushing the bar from nanometers to centimeters. All we need is another order of magnitude, and we can finally observe Schrödinger's cat in real life."
Scientists tested 5 natural compounds on cancer cells. One stood out
Curcumin and berberine disrupted cancer cell energy production and stopped many fibrosarcoma cells from dividing.

- Five natural compounds, including curcumin and berberine, were tested for their effects on cancer cells and healthy muscle cells. All disrupted cancer cell energy production and pushed many of the cells into a non-dividing state, with curcumin producing the strongest overall effect. Curcumin also showed a relatively favorable safety profile, while some other compounds caused more toxicity.

Curcumin, berberine, and several other plant-derived substances have drawn attention from scientists because of their potential anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects. New research from Wroclaw Medical University and the University of Wroclaw suggests, however, that these compounds can behave very differently. A substance that appears powerful against cancer cells may not necessarily have the best safety profile.

The researchers examined five compounds: curcumin, berberine, biochanin A, cucurbitacin E, and CAPE (caffeic acid phenethyl ester), a component of propolis. They compared how each one affected fibrosarcoma cells and healthy muscle cells.
How Natural Compounds Affect a Key Cellular Pathway
A major focus of the study was the NF-κB signaling pathway, which helps regulate inflammation, metabolism, cell survival, and cellular aging.

"NF-κB acts like a central control switch that integrates cellular stress signals and determines whether a cell activates inflammatory pathways, fights for survival or changes its metabolism," explains Prof. Julita Kulbacka from the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology at Wroclaw Medical University.

In cancer cells, unusually high NF-κB activity can help cells survive and adjust to stressful conditions. But the pathway also plays an important role in healthy cells. That means an ideal strategy would not eliminate NF-κB activity altogether, but instead influence it in a more controlled and selective way.
Cancer Cells Were More Vulnerable to Energy Loss
The five compounds also interfered with mitochondrial function, making it harder for cells to generate energy.

The effect was especially pronounced in fibrosarcoma cells. Their ATP levels fell by approximately 83-92%, while healthy muscle cells experienced decreases of around 23-73%. The difference suggests that cancer cells may be particularly vulnerable when their energy metabolism is disrupted.
The compounds also changed mitophagy, the process cells use to remove damaged mitochondria.

"Berberine, cucurbitacin E and CAPE enhanced PINK1/PARKIN-dependent mitophagy in fibrosarcoma cells. Combined with the marked reduction in ATP levels, this indicates not a protective response but an overwhelmed adaptive mechanism leading to cellular senescence and death," says Prof. Julita Kulbacka.
Natural Compounds Pushed Cancer Cells Into Senescence
All five compounds triggered signs of cellular senescence in fibrosarcoma cells. Senescent cells remain alive, but they permanently lose the ability to continue dividing.
Curcumin produced the strongest effect. The share of senescent cancer cells rose from approximately 16.5% to more than 75%. Each of the other compounds also pushed the percentage above 66%.
Healthy muscle cells generally responded less strongly, indicating that the compounds showed some degree of selectivity toward cancer cells.
Curcumin Offered the Best Overall Balance

Cell viability tests showed that curcumin and CAPE were the most selective against fibrosarcoma cells. Curcumin stood out because it combined strong anticancer activity and induction of cellular senescence with a comparatively favorable safety profile.

"Our findings show that these natural compounds can selectively place a greater metabolic burden on cancer cells than on healthy cells by disrupting mitochondrial function and energy metabolism. Among the compounds tested, curcumin demonstrated the most balanced profile," emphasizes Prof. Julita Kulbacka.
Berberine was also well tolerated. However, researchers say its effects on mitochondria in healthy muscle cells still need to be studied in greater detail.
Anticancer Activity Is Only Part of the Picture
To get an early look at safety beyond isolated cells, the researchers also tested the compounds in greater wax moth (Galleria mellonella) larvae.
Curcumin and berberine were the best tolerated. CAPE and cucurbitacin E were associated with higher mortality, while biochanin A was the most toxic of the five compounds.
The results underscore an important point in drug development. A compound can be highly active against cancer cells and still be a poor candidate if it causes too much harm elsewhere in the organism.
These Compounds Are Not Cancer Treatments Yet

The findings do not show that curcumin, berberine, or the other compounds can currently be used to treat sarcomas. The experiments relied on animal cell lines and a relatively simple invertebrate toxicity model.

"Our findings come from laboratory experiments and preliminary tests in wax moth larvae. The next step is to evaluate these compounds in more advanced in vivo models and to better understand their mechanisms of action, optimal dosing and delivery methods," notes Prof. Kulbacka.

Even so, the work helps narrow down which natural compounds may deserve closer study. It also shows why potential anticancer agents should be judged not only by how effectively they affect cancer cells, but also by how they influence healthy tissues and the organism as a whole.
- Sarcomas account for less than 1% of all cancers in adults but include more than 100 different disease subtypes.
- There is no single treatment that works for all sarcomas. Different subtypes often require different therapeutic approaches.
- Cancer cells consume much more energy than most healthy cells.
- When their "power plants" -- the mitochondria -- stop functioning properly, their ability to grow and divide is impaired.
- Natural compounds may inspire the development of future medicines, but they are not therapies on their own.

Nearly 30,000 people tested quit-smoking methods. One stood out

Nicotine e-cigarettes are more effective in helping people quit smoking than many conventional methods such as nicotine gums and patches and quitting with behavioral support or no support at all, an updated Cochrane review finds

- Nicotine e-cigarettes appear to help more smokers quit than patches, gum, and several other common approaches, according to a major review of 80 clinical trials. Researchers say regulated vaping products are not risk-free, but may be a significantly less harmful alternative for people who would otherwise continue smoking.

An updated Cochrane review has found that nicotine e-cigarettes may help more people stop smoking than several commonly used approaches, including nicotine gum, nicotine patches, behavioral support, or trying to quit without assistance.

Smoking remains the world's leading cause of preventable disease and death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), it is responsible for more than seven million deaths each year, including 1.6 million deaths among non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke.

The findings come from a living systematic review, meaning researchers continually update the analysis as new evidence becomes available. The latest version included 80 randomized controlled trials involving 29,861 participants, with nine new trials added in this update.
Nicotine Vapes Outperform Patches and Gum

The researchers found high-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes produced higher quit rates than nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), such as patches and gum. For every 100 people, nicotine e-cigarettes resulted in about 4 additional people successfully quitting.
Nicotine e-cigarettes also performed better than non-nicotine cigarettes, leading to about 2 additional quitters per 100 people.

People given e-cigarettes also had higher quit rates than those who received no support or behavioral support (such as individual counseling and group programs). However, the researchers had less confidence in this comparison because of potential bias in how some of the studies were designed.

"We have very strong evidence that regulated nicotine e-cigarettes are substantially less harmful than smoking," says Dr. Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, senior author of the review from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. "Based on the consistency of the findings here, it's clear that they are a proven and viable option for people wishing to quit traditional cigarettes. This update includes 9 new trials and our main conclusions haven't changed."
What the Evidence Says About Vaping Risks
Researchers found no evidence that using e-cigarettes to quit smoking increased the risk of serious harm, although they emphasize that longer-term research is still needed.
The conclusions apply specifically to regulated, nicotine-containing e-cigarettes. Illicit products and e-cigarettes containing other substances, such as THC, may present different risks.

"It's worth highlighting that our review looks at regulated e-cigarettes containing nicotine, but many of those available on the market do not meet these standards," says Dr. Hartmann-Boyce. "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals. Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body. Lists of regulated devices are available from the FDA in the US and MHRA in the UK."

Major health organizations and agencies, including the WHO, continue to warn that e-cigarettes expose users to nicotine and other chemicals that can be harmful. Health officials have also raised concerns that e-cigarette use among children and young people can lead to nicotine addiction and later use of tobacco products.
A Step Away From Cigarettes, Not a Risk-Free Endpoint

The researchers stress that e-cigarettes may not be the best quitting method for everyone. People who want to stop smoking are encouraged to speak with stop-smoking support services or their clinicians about the most appropriate approach.
Vaping still carries health risks. However, the authors say those risks are much smaller than the dangers associated with continuing to smoke cigarettes.

Dr. Nicola Lindson, lead author of the review based at the University of Oxford, reflects that: "Quitting smoking is hard, and a lot of people who smoke will have tried many times to quit smoking and been unsuccessful. For that reason, it is important that there are a number of different options available to help somebody quit, which could encourage them to keep trying. Although nicotine vapes are unlikely to be completely risk-free, they are less harmful than smoking, and that is the most important comparison to make for people who are still smoking tobacco."
Dr. Hartmann-Boyce views switching to e-cigarettes as a possible stage in the process of moving away from smoking, rather than necessarily the final destination.

"For somebody who is already addicted to nicotine through cigarettes, having a safer alternative like an e-cigarette is something worth considering, especially when other quit aids have proven unsuccessful. We are currently working on a review of interventions to help people quit vaping, which could be the next step along for people looking to transition to a lower-harm product before quitting nicotine altogether."

Octoberâs night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats

- Octoberâs skies are packed with celestial surprises, from Jupiter disappearing behind the Moon to two meteor showers lighting up the darkness. NASA highlights four must-see events, including shooting stars from Halleyâs Comet and a glowing Hunterâs Moon just before Halloween.

October is bringing a spectacular lineup of celestial events, including a disappearing planet, two meteor showers, and a bright full Moon just in time for Halloween. As autumn days grow shorter and darkness arrives earlier, the night sky offers more opportunities to witness some remarkable astronomical sights.

NASA has highlighted four events worth watching this month, ranging from Jupiter briefly vanishing behind the Moon to shooting stars created by debris from Halley's Comet. With crisp autumn evenings and a little luck, skywatchers can enjoy several of these displays without any special equipment.
Jupiter Disappears Behind the Moon on October 6

Before sunrise on Tuesday, October 6, skywatchers in parts of North America had an opportunity to witness an unusual celestial disappearing act. Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, slipped behind the Moon's slender crescent and remained hidden for approximately an hour before coming back into view.

Astronomers call this phenomenon a lunar occultation. It happens when the Moon moves directly between Earth and a more distant object, temporarily blocking our view. Despite its mysterious-sounding name, occultation simply refers to one celestial object concealing another.

The event was visible to the naked eye, although binoculars offered a more detailed look. Observers using optical equipment could also potentially watch some of Jupiter's moons disappear behind the lunar edge and emerge again.

Viewing opportunities depended on location, with the occultation visible across parts of eastern and central North America. The timing varied geographically, with the event occurring during the early morning hours, around 4 a.m. EDT in some locations.
Draconid Meteor Shower Peaks October 8 and 9

The next celestial attraction comes on the evening of Thursday, October 8, when the Draconid meteor shower reaches its peak. Favorable viewing beginning around 9 p.m. EDT, and the display continues into the early hours of Friday, October 9.

Unlike many meteor showers that are best observed after midnight, the Draconids offer a convenient opportunity to see shooting stars soon after nightfall. That makes them particularly appealing to casual observers who would rather not stay awake until dawn.
Conditions are especially promising this year because the Moon is approaching its new phase. With little moonlight to brighten the sky, even relatively faint meteors should be easier to detect.

The shower gets its name from Draco, a constellation representing a dragon. Although the name might sound like something from a Halloween horror story involving a certain famous vampire, it actually refers to the constellation from which the meteors appear to originate.

The Draconids are generally a modest display, typically producing only a handful of visible meteors each hour. For the best chance of spotting them, head somewhere away from bright city lights, allow your eyes to adjust to the darkness, and scan the open sky for brief streaks of light.
Orionid Meteor Shower Brings Debris From Halley's Comet
Another opportunity to catch shooting stars arrives on October 21, when the Orionid meteor shower reaches its annual peak.

These meteors have a particularly fascinating origin. They are tiny fragments of material left behind by Halley's Comet during its journeys through the solar system. When Earth travels through this trail of ancient comet debris, the particles enter our atmosphere at tremendous speeds, creating bright streaks of light as they burn up.

For observers in suburban areas with some artificial lighting, NASA estimates that approximately 3 to 6 meteors may be visible each hour. People watching from darker locations could see somewhat more.

The Orionids take their name from Orion, the famous hunter constellation, because their meteors appear to radiate from that region of the sky. Orion is also home to Betelgeuse, an enormous red supergiant star recognizable by its reddish appearance (but don't say that name three times in a row!).

There is one potential obstacle to this year's display. The Moon will be in its waxing gibbous phase, meaning more than half of its visible surface will be illuminated. Its brightness could make some of the dimmer meteors difficult to spot.

Fortunately, viewing conditions should improve after the Moon sets at approximately 3 a.m. local time. By then, Orion will also be higher in the sky, creating a better opportunity to catch meteors during the hours before sunrise.
October's Hunter's Moon Lights Up the Halloween Sky

October's final major celestial highlight is the Hunter's Moon, which reaches its full phase on October 26 in Universal Time. For observers in much of North America, the Moon will appear full on the evening of Sunday, October 25.

The name Hunter's Moon comes from traditions associated with the changing autumn season. As crops were harvested, fields became more open, and daylight hours shortened, hunters could take advantage of the bright moonlight to locate and follow animals after sunset.

The Moon will remain a prominent feature of the night sky in the days following its full phase. As Halloween approaches, it will gradually transition into a waning gibbous Moon, with its illuminated portion slowly decreasing each night.
Its lingering glow will provide a fitting backdrop for the final evenings of October, bringing NASA's month of celestial tricks and treats to a memorable close.

From soft peeps to piercing calls, birds produce a wide range of sounds. But scientists recently discovered that two South American species take their calls to ear-splitting extremes, making deafening vocalizations on par with a jackhammer.

The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema can produce sounds at amplitudes that exceed 120 decibels, according to a study published September 29 in the journal Evolution. They’re now among the ranks of the white bellbird, another South American species, for the loudest known birds on the planet.

Researchers behind the new work didn’t specifically set out to find the world’s noisiest birds. Rather, they wanted to take advantage of recent technological advancements that have made it easier to measure vocal amplitude, the height of a sound wave and a key element of loudness.

“Until recently, it was very impractical to go out into the field and measure amplitude,” lead author João Menezes, an evolutionary biologist who conducted the research while at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tells the New York Times’ Taylor Mitchell Brown. “It’s kind of stepping into a whole new world.”

The researchers started the project in Amherst, Massachusetts, during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when the unusually quiet circumstances made it easier to isolate and record bird song. They used a laser rangefinder to measure their distance from a specific bird, as well as a sound level meter, which allowed them to isolate that bird’s call from other noises.

“Even recording from my window or from the backyard, almost always that would be [the amplitude of] a new species,” Menezes tells the Washington Post’s Meghan Bartels. “It’s not often that you get to do this kind of exploratory science where you just go out into the field and document things for the first time, especially with birds.”

From Massachusetts, they headed next to Brazil, where they recorded birds in several different habitats. The scientists ultimately collected amplitude data on 123 bird species between December 2018 and January 2025, filling a major gap in scientists’ understanding of how loud birds can sing. Previously, scientists only had amplitude data for ten of those species—even the ubiquitous Canada goose had never been measured.

“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” study co-author Jeffrey Podos, also an evolutionary biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says in a statement. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale.”

Their amplitude database captures the impressive range of bird vocalization volumes. At the low end, they documented the dusky-throated hermit, a hummingbird that buzzes at a modest 64 decibels, about the same volume as a normal conversation. At the high end, the bare-throated bellbird and red-legged seriema are both about as loud as a trumpeting elephant or a chainsaw.

Comparing the amplitude data with the birds’ anatomy revealed that species with bigger bodies and wider mouth openings also tended to be the loudest. This is probably because “bigger birds have bulkier muscles, which are capable of creating greater internal pressures, which ultimately generate louder sounds, and then broader mouths allow more energy to radiate into the environment,” Menezes tells CNN’s Amarachi Orie.

Still, the researchers have many unanswered questions. The big one: Why are some birds so much louder than others? The researchers hypothesized that the loudest birds evolved their high-volume calls to attract numerous mates, or to communicate through dense vegetation. But those explanations don’t hold up for the red-legged seriema, so there must be some other factor driving the evolution of its loud vocalizations.

“The seriema is the opposite of those two things,” Menezes tells WBUR’s Barbara Moran. “It’s a super open-habitat bird, like pasture, and it’s strictly monogamous. So, it forms a pair for the breeding season, and that’s it.”

There’s no single answer to the question of which species holds the title of “world’s loudest bird”—it depends on how researchers define loudness. The bare-throated bellbird, for example, produced the loudest individual call, reaching nearly 131 decibels, per CNN. But when researchers averaged the loudest calls across individual birds, the red-legged seriema came out on top at nearly 121 decibels. Averaging the vocalizations’ peak volumes, on the other hand, allowed the white bellbird to take the lead at 127 decibels.

Scientists are still unraveling the evolutionary underpinnings of super loud birdsong. But in the meantime, their work could have important implications for conservation. For example, reliable amplitude data could help researchers use audio recordings to determine not just whether a species is present, but also how close those birds might be and how many individuals are nearby, Connor Wood, an ornithologist at Cornell University who wasn’t involved in the study, tells the Washington Post.
The findings could also help scientists better understand how birds may adapt to a changing world.

“Amplitude is so critical to the ability of birds to communicate with each other, that it is really important for us to understand exactly how that might be able to change,” Nathan Senner, an ornithologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst who also wasn’t involved with the study, tells WBUR. “How they evolve is really fundamental to our understanding of how they might continue to evolve as our world changes.”

Historians have long known that Lismore, a small isle in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, was home to a medieval monastery called Lios Mòr. Written records detail its sixth-century founding by St. Mo Luóc, one of the early monks who spread Christianity to northern Britain. But with very little archaeological evidence, apart from a broken granite cross, scholars could not confirm Lios Mòr’s size, style or significance—until now.

According to an article published in the journal Antiquity last week, a group of local volunteers led by archaeologist Clare Ellis, of the firm Argyll Archaeology, discovered an early medieval cemetery, various structures and “sophisticated craftworking of international importance” during excavations near Lismore’s 13th-century parish church.

“For centuries, Lismore’s early monastery was known mainly from written records and local tradition,” study co-author Gordon Noble, an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen, says in a statement. “We can now see that it was a thriving center of worship, craftsmanship and learning, whose importance may have rivaled some of the best-known monasteries in early medieval Britain.”

Lismore’s historical society began searching for the site of Mo Luóc’s monastery in 2016. A “dynamic minority” of the island’s 170 or so residents crowdfunded and ran the digs, Robert Hay, a retired local scientist and dig participant, tells the Guardian’s Esther Addley. Grants, donations and yet more crowdfunding enabled the enthusiastic locals to hire Ellis to lead excavations near the site of Lismore’s 13th-century church, which still holds services.

“The research aimed to determine whether the site of the later medieval cathedral at Lismore was also the location of Mo Luóc’s early monastery, and to assess the scale, nature and status of the settlement,” Ellis says in the statement.

The dig uncovered a medieval cemetery containing at least six burials radiocarbon dated to between 650 and 1040 C.E. The archaeologists also unearthed a piece of an “early medieval cross slab,” per the study. In another area, they found more human remains and additional fragments of carved stone crosses.

“This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment,” Noble tells the Guardian. He compares it to Scotland’s famed Iona monastery, which was founded in 563 C.E. Both settlements were products of a medieval missionary movement that aimed to spread Christianity throughout pagan Britain. The monks succeeded. By the seventh century, Britain was Christianized.

Elsewhere on the cathedral property, researchers found the remains of an oval-shaped building paved with a layer of limestone. Dated to between the seventh and tenth centuries, it contained remnants of craftwork, handmade pottery, struck flint and an antler.

Another trench boasted extensive evidence of precious metalwork: more than 1,000 pieces of debris, including well-preserved molds and crucibles once used to melt down and cast gold, copper and silver. Hay describes them as “the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland,” per the Guardian.

Clay molds and crucibles are “unusual” finds for a monastic site, Noble tells Scientific American’s Jackie Flynn Mogensen. “It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he adds.

The Lismore monastery appears to have an unusually large footprint. This, coupled with evidence of precious metals and craftsmanship, suggests the community was actually considerably wealthy and “far more than a small island church,” per the statement.
As Noble says to Scientific American, Lios Mòr appears to have been “a very significant mover and shaker” in its day. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”
In September, the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at 10.6 million square miles—the second largest ever observed for this time of year.

Using data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, scientists found that the ozone hole started growing earlier than usual in August. By September 20, it reached a size close to its October 2015 peak, when it was 10.8 million square miles.

To understand what’s happening, we first need to understand the ozone layer. The ozone layer lies in the Earth’s stratosphere and protects our planet from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation that can harm humans, plants and animals. The infamous ozone hole is actually a patch of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over Antarctica that is mainly caused by chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. While the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the use of CFCs globally, they can persist in the atmosphere for decades.

The ozone hole’s size fluctuates every year. For about three months each fall—the Southern Hemisphere’s spring—the hole opens inside the stratospheric polar vortex, a large band of fast-spinning westerly winds that encircles Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. The vortex traps freezing air inside and leads to the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, writes a New Zealand-based research team in The Conversation. “Chemical reactions on particles in this rare type of cloud then activate ozone-depleting gases,” they add.

This year brought a stronger and colder polar vortex. “We have unusually strong winds and cold temperatures over the pole that have created the conditions possible for the hole to grow to the size it has today,” research team member Hannah Kessenich, a physicist at the University of Otago in New Zealand, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC News). By late January, the hole will shrink again.
Did you know? Wildfires can destroy the ozone layer

- Climate change has increased the frequency of wildfires, which is not a good thing when it comes to mending the ozone layer. A study published in Nature in 2023 found that particles in wildfire smoke spark chemical reactions in the atmosphere that break down ozone.

So, should we be worried? “This year’s ozone hole shouldn’t be a cause for alarm,” Kessenich told Live Science's Sascha Pare in an email. “However, there are still many unanswered questions. It’s something we need to keep a close eye on.”

Kessenich and other experts underscore the fact that the ozone hole size we’re currently seeing isn’t a sign that the Montreal Protocol isn’t working. “We look at the depth of the hole rather than the area to assess how we’re coming along in terms of the recovery from those chemicals,” Kessenich says to ABC News.

In fact, this year’s hole isn’t as deep as it has been in previous years, and year-to-year variability is to be expected. “We have to look at the longer term trends, and those metrics continue to tell us that the ozone hole is slowly recovering as expected,” adds Susan Solomon, an atmospheric chemist at MIT, in an email to Live Science.

There will, however, be impacts on weather across the Southern Hemisphere. A larger ozone hole shifts the Southern Annular Mode into a positive phase, which affects winds and precipitation in different areas. In Australia, for example, it causes increased rainfall on the country’s southeast coast, Kessenich and her colleagues write in The Conversation.

Researchers are still trying to understand how climate change impacts the strength of the polar vortex, and why bigger ozone holes are persisting longer than they used to. It could be that changes in global atmospheric dynamics are making longer-lived ozone holes more likely, which in turn could mean our timelines for ozone recovery need to be adapted.
“It's too soon to tell what has been driving dynamical variability in recent years, but more research is needed,” Kessenich says to Live Science.

NEW YORK, Oct. 10 (UPI) -- The Walking Dead legends Norman Reedus and Melissa McBride appeared at New York Comic Con Friday to talk about their 15-year journey as zombie-apocalypse survivors Daryl and Carol.
The stars played the best friends for 11 seasons of the flagship TWD series, which took place in the American southwest, and for four seasons of the European spin-off, Daryl Dixon.
Season 4 has already been filmed and premieres in February. The final season is being billed as "one last journey, one last fight."
"It was super-weird, the whole last week [of filming,]" Reedus, 57, told UPI at a New York Comic Con press conference Friday.

"Not to give spoilers away in any way, whatsoever. But it was sad. It was an accomplishment. It felt like that quote from David Bowie, when they say, 'What do you think your last words are going to be when you die?' And he goes, 'But, but, but...' It was a little bit like that," the actor recalled.

"But it felt like an accomplishment. It felt like we told the story we were trying to tell and it was sad for the crew, too. You become this really big family, especially when we're going overseas and hanging around new people in a new place and it was very emotional all the way."

"There were three things: there was Melissa's last scene and there was Norman's last scene and there's the last scene they did together," executive producer David Zabel said. "So, there's sort of three things, each of which was emotionally different."
McBride added, "And Norman's last scene was the last shot we ever shot as a show."
Zabel said that just because this chapter of The Walking Dead is over, doesn't mean there aren't still stories in this universe to tell.
"There will still be shows," executive producer Scott M. Gimple said. "See what's in them."
Oct. 10 (UPI) -- Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt, was released from the hospital Saturday, 10 days later.
She was transferred back to the prison in Nashville where she was held before her execution.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement Saturday. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."
Pike, 50, was the first woman Tennessee tried to execute in more than 200 years on Sept. 30. She received two doses of pentobarbital, each of which could have been lethal.

Pike survived the injections and was seen by witnesses snoring and breathing. She was taken to the hospital in critical condition and unconscious. Her lawyers had believed she was brain dead, but she woke up and began speaking on Oct. 6. On Thursday, her lawyer said she was up and walking in the hospital.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt after getting a lethal injection in the United States.

Pike, along with her then-boyfriend and another young woman, tortured and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, in 1995. Pike, who was 18, is the only one of the three with a death sentence. The boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was ineligible for the death penalty because he was 17. The other woman, Shadolla Peterson, testified against Pike and Shipp and was given probation.
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- Hurricane Isaias landed near Destin, Fla., Friday evening, and was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone, bringing high winds, rain and flooding.
One person in Escambia County, Fla., died "due to a downed tree," county officials said, and another was killed in Birmingham, Ala. Both were killed when trees fell on homes.
Across the southeastern United States, about 860,000 people were without power Saturday, with trees and power lines down.
Emergency management in Santa Rosa County, Fla., situated between Pensacola and Destin, said the majority of roads in the county are "impassable due to down trees and/or power lines."
More than 80% of customers were without power, and wind gusts rose to more than 100 mph Friday night.
Thirty teams from the Florida Department of Transportation are assessing damage Saturday in the Panhandle.

"At first light, thousands of linemen and utility crews have convoyed from Sandestin and along the I-10 corridor to get to work, focusing on outages in the hardest hit communities," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said.
"It was pitch black out. The storm had passed. It was safe enough to go out, and they were doing it," he added.
Some airports in the area have reopened. Northwest Florida Beaches Airport reopened to commercial service, but the Destin, Fort Walton Beach and Pensacola airports are still closed.

Heavy rainfall will move quickly into the Tennessee Valley and southern Appalachians. Flash flooding and landslides are possible, especially in mountainous areas, the National Hurricane Center said in its 4 a.m. CDT Saturday update.
Isaias was about 105 miles south of Birmingham, Ala., and about 25 miles south-southeast of Mobile, with maximum sustained winds of about 35 mph. There are no more weather warnings in effect.
Isaias is the first hurricane of the year in the Atlantic basin, despite a strong El Niño.
Through the weekend, Isaias is expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rainfall across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, the Big Bend region and southwest Georgia.
Localized totals up to 15 inches were also possible across the Panhandle and Big Bend.
Forecasters expected the coastal Carolinas to receive 2 to 5 inches of rain, with localized totals up to 10 inches also possible.
The remainder of the Southeast was forecast to get 2 to 5 inches. A risk for tornadoes will persist through Saturday afternoon across parts of the eastern Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.
Wind shear in the Atlantic has kept hurricanes at bay so far this season, but low wind shear in the Gulf helped Isaias.

Noordwijk, the Netherlands | September 22, 2026 – During the international Industry Space Days 2026 event at the European Space Agency’s ESTEC facility in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, the Latvian Mobile Telephone (LMT) Group and the globally leading space consultancy Novaspace signed a cooperation agreement on the development of a concept for telecommunications innovation platform for Latvia to link the national connectivity sector with the international satellite industry. The initiative follows the successful ESA 5G/6G Non-Terrestrial Network Hub model and will explore Latvia’s potential role within this network.

Signing the agreement marks a pivotal step toward creating a hub for developing an internationally competitive telecommunications sector in Latvia. The hub will strategically bring LMT into the space industry and impact the emergence of a wider Latvia’s space innovation ecosystem in next-generation satellite technologies, products, and services tailored to commercial applications, resilient critical infrastructure, security, digitalization and green transition. Essentially, the hub will attract national and international cooperation, funding and talent.

The next generation of mobile communications is closely linked to the rapid growth of the space economy globally. The space infrastructure is already gradually enhancing terrestrial networks, and the 6G era of telecommunications will seamlessly link terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks. The rationale for such development is efficient and resilient connectivity, especially essential in scenarios involving severe weather, power outages or physical infrastructure disruptions.

This initiative builds upon LMT Group’s strategic expansion of its track record in connectivity innovation. LMT is already collaborating with ESA and satellite operator Sateliot to pioneer energy efficient dual-mode satellite Internet of Things (IoT) connectivity, enabled by Latvia’s associate membership in ESA. The hardware and software to be developed will cover the current market gap in devices that can seamlessly switch between terrestrial and satellite networks. The planned 5G/6G NTN hub is a natural next step in scaling LMT’s technological footprint within Europe’s space ecosystem.

“LMT has long evolved beyond traditional mobile operations into a full-scale technology innovator. As we prepare for the 6G era, integrating satellite communications into our infrastructure and service portfolio is essential. Our goal is to ensure resilient, secure communications for new commercial services and for critical infrastructure under any circumstances, to produce exportable space technologies and develop services that contribute to digitalization and green transition. Partnering with Novaspace will allow us to define Latvia’s unique value proposition within the European space ecosystem and expand local high-tech expertise,” Ingmārs Pūķis, VP & Member of the Management Board at LMT.

The agreement was signed under the EU-funded FIERCE Ecosystem Building Programme, in which LMT participates as an innovation intermediary and Novaspace provides strategic support and space-market expertise. Through the programme, Novaspace will work directly with LMT to define and validate the concept, guiding LMT towards a Latvian 5G/6G terrestrial and non-terrestrial network (TN/NTN) hub. The joint effort will focus on identifying Latvia’s distinctive regional value proposition and connecting the future hub with the wider European 5G/6G and NTN ecosystem, rather than replicating existing European initiatives.

“At Novaspace, we are delighted to partner with LMT Group through the FIERCE project. The strength of Europe’s space sector depends on active participation across all Member States, and Latvia is well positioned both to benefit from and contribute to Europe’s growing space economy. Flagship European programmes such as Copernicus, Galileo, EGNOS and IRIS² are creating new opportunities for innovation, resilient connectivity and commercial growth. Drawing on Novaspace’s global market expertise, we look forward to supporting LMT in defining a distinctive role for Latvia within Europe’s 5G/6G and non-terrestrial network ecosystem,” Gabrielle Brophy, Senior Manager at Novaspace.

The planned hub will be developed together with research and industry partners in the region. This collaborative framework will help retain and grow specialized engineering and scientific competencies in the Baltic region.

The signing ceremony in Noordwijk was attended by representatives of the European Space Agency, Novaspace, the Latvian embassy in the Netherlands, the Ministry of Education and Science of the Republic of Latvia, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia, Novaspace in representation of the FIERCE project and LMT.

Ukraine: UN condemns latest attacks and calls for civilian protection

The UN Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine on Wednesday called for an end to attacks against civilians following further overnight strikes by Russian forces that reportedly killed at least 19 in the Chernihiv Region.
Among the dead in Pryluky were five children, three of them babies, according to the latest information from local authorities. One of the children died along with his mother and grandmother.
At least 50 others were reportedly injured when residential buildings were struck. The casualty toll is expected to rise as rescue operations continue.
The overnight wave of attacks also reportedly killed around 25 others and injured dozens of civilians in Kremenchuk in the Poltava region, Kyiv and Oleksandriia in the Kirovohrad region.
According to the latest data, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year.

“Families must never live through the horror of seeing their children placed in constant danger or buried under the rubble of their own homes. This pattern of increasing harm to civilians must end,” the UN’s top official in the country Matthias Schmale said in a statement.
On 5 and 6 October, airstrikes hit a hospital in Kryvyi Rih and ambulances in Kramatorsk, injuring health workers.
Ukrainian Red Cross workers were also injured while travelling to assist people affected by an attack in Zaporizhzhia.
“Civilians, including children, homes and essential civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law,” Mr. Schmale reiterated.

Briefing journalists in New York Wednesday, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the Secretary-General strongly condemned the ongoing attacks. He also expressed deep concern over the rising number of civilian casualties.
“All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately,” Mr. Dujarric said.
Humanitarian teams in Ukraine reported that attacks and frontline hostilities over the previous 24 hours had caused more than 150 civilian casualties.

During the first eight months of this year, the UN and its humanitarian partners assisted 1.5 million people affected by strikes across Ukraine, as attacks continue to intensify and spread to areas farther from the front lines.
UN rights chief: Legacy of slavery and colonialism is still fuelling racism

The legacy of enslavement and colonialism continues to shape the lives of Africans and people of African descent, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Thursday, calling for urgent action to deliver reparatory justice beyond financial compensation.
Over 30 million people were violently uprooted from Africa and condemned to a life of slavery.
Yet no country involved in enslavement or colonialism has fully confronted this past.

Speaking at a high-level dialogue on reparatory Justice in Geneva, Mr. Türk said the transatlantic trade was an organised system of domination that treated tens of millions of African men, women and children as commodities.
Women and girls suffered particularly grave abuses, including sexual and gender-based violence, he underscored.

Reiterating that the legacy of these injustices lives on today, Mr. Türk told delegates that “their consequences – together with those of colonialism more generally – continue to shape who has opportunity, security, and power – and who does not.”

Calls for reparatory justice have been growing, said High Commissioner Türk. Some States, universities, religious groups and businesses have begun to confront their historic role in African enslavement.
Racism can be encountered in everyday life, from employment and housing to education and healthcare, the UN rights chief said.

In some regions, police are several times more likely to use force against people of African descent, while people of the dispora are also disproportionately represented in prisons and criminal justice systems.
Mr. Türk also warned that emerging technologies could compound existing inequalities.

“Artificial intelligence and other technologies are already reproducing human biases,” he said. “If we are not careful, they could deepen systemic racism against Africans and people of African descent.”
Mr. Türk stressed that reparatory justice should not be understood as financial compensation alone.

Instead, it should include confronting the truth about the past, formal apologies, truth-seeking initiatives and memorials recognising the experiences and contributions of Africans and people of African descent.
Other measures can include the restitution of cultural artefacts, compensation, education and awareness-raising, as well as medical and psychosocial support to address intergenerational trauma.
The UN rights office (OHCHR) has developed a series of explainers to help States advance reparatory justice, highlighting key measures and examples of action, including apologies.

“No State has fully accounted for the harms of the past or systemic racism today,” he continued noting that many countries still lack anti-racism legislation and that fewer than one in four have comprehensive anti-discrimination laws.

Calling for stronger implementation of existing laws and targeted investment to remove barriers affecting access to healthcare, housing, education, justice and employment, he said that Africans and people of African descent, particularly women, must be at the centre of reparatory efforts.

Mr. Türk urged reforms to the international financial architecture, including measures to ease unsustainable debt and strengthen the participation of African countries in international decision-making.
“A child born in 2026 should not have to carry the weight of centuries of racial discrimination and the horrors of the past,” he concluded.
Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
She was honoured “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement.

The committee said the award was going “to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order,” noting that she “has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.”

Ms. Pillay served as the UN human rights chief from September 2008 through August 2014, but her career has spanned more than 50 years - from fighting apartheid in her homeland to defending civilians in conflict zones.

She is a former chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and was appointed a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, in addition to serving as an ad hoc judge with the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's highest court.

“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the Nobel Committee said.
An ‘independent voice of justice’: Guterres

In a statement congratulating the new Nobel laureate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Ms. Pillay has shown “that the force of law must prevail over the law of force and that defending human rights is the surest safeguard against injustice.”

He hailed her as “a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice”, adding that “in its citation, the Nobel Committee reminded the world that peace must be built on lasting principles, not the will of the powerful."
Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was born in South Africa in 1941 to a Tamil Indian family and was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country.
As a lawyer, she acted as a defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists, exposing torture, and helping to establish key rights for prisoners on notorious Robben Island.

In her role as chair of the Independent International Commission, which is appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, she oversaw its 2025 report that said Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip constituted genocide.
