On receiving the news of Ms. Pillay's honour, the current UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warmly congratulated the woman he described as a big sister.

“To say it is well deserved is a total understatement, and especially at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power, this award is particularly poignant,” he said, speaking in Geneva.
“It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security.”
Moreover, it is “a recognition, a reaffirmation, that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything - to peace, to security and prosperity,” he added.
In an October 2025 interview with UN News in Geneva, Ms. Pillay reflected on her lifetime of fighting for human rights, justice and equality.

“I didn't think apartheid would end in my lifetime,” she recalled. “So, what happened? We had the collective support of people all over the world, even children. If we can achieve that, we can have a better human rights protection system.”

Her experience in the anti-apartheid struggle shaped her belief in international solidarity, which she carried into her role as a judge and president of the ITCR, which prosecuted persons responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
During her eight years there, she helped establish groundbreaking legal precedents in the fight against genocide and gender-based violence.
As UN human rights chief, Ms. Pillay continued to champion the participation of civil society and victims’ voices in shaping global human rights standards.

“When the UN started, it was just a club for the States,” she told UN News. “Everything we have today for human rights protection didn’t happen just because the States woke up one day. It comes from the pressure of civil society. That’s why I value these institutions.”

LONDON — A British Airways passenger jet flying from London to Chicago descended 28,000 feet in just seven minutes after declaring an emergency due to an unspecified “technical issue,” the airline said Monday.
The Boeing 777 took off at 12:15 p.m. local time (7:15 a.m. ET) but started descending just 30 minutes later while flying over Ireland, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

The plane turned around and spent around four hours zigzagging over the Bristol Channel, a waterway to the west of England, before landing back at London Heathrow Airport at 5 p.m. local time (noon ET).

“The aircraft landed safely after our highly-trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue,” British Airways said in an emailed statement. “Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.”
Heathrow did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Passengers will likely be put up in hotels by the airline until another flight can be arranged, as stipulated by the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.

Britain’s National Air Traffic Service (NATS) came under scrutiny last month after two technical problems in the space of two weeks caused major delays at several U.K. airports and hundreds of flights were canceled.
NATS blamed software issues for the delays.
Britain’s Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation had been “deeply frustrating” for passengers.
With 84.5 million passengers last year, Heathrow ranked seventh in the table of the world’s busiest airports, according to data published by Airports Council International.
Travel from Heathrow was severely disrupted in March last year when a massive fire at an electricity substation caused a predawn power outage at the global transport hub.
The closure affected more than 1,300 flights and 200,000 passengers.

After investigating 600 items of evidence related to the substation, the National Energy System Operator ruled out suspicious activity in a report saying a preventable moisture fault caused the fire, leaving almost 70,000 homes without power.

Around 4,500 years ago, ancient Egyptians carved the Great Sphinx of Giza out of limestone in the Mokattam rock formation. Little did they know, the material they were digging through preserved something even more archaic: fossils of a long-extinct crocodile.

Researchers have identified a previously unknown species of gavial, a type of crocodilian with a long, thin snout, from a fossil originally found in the rock formation that the ancient Egyptians sculpted into the Sphinx and the Pyramids of Giza. The new identification corrects a previous erroneous classification, according to a study published October 7 in the journal Royal Society Open Science. It also sheds light on the fauna that existed in what’s now Egypt well before human-made monuments appeared on the horizon.

In the 1920s, several fossilized remains, including a largely intact crocodile-like skull, emerged from the roughly 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation at a site near Cairo. Because of the bones’ resemblance to those of Tomistoma schlegelii—a living gavial native to Indonesia and Malaysia—experts originally assigned them to the same Tomistoma genus. Until now, the well-preserved skull was the holotype, or name-bearing representative fossil, for the extinct T. cairense.

Thanks to modern paleontological techniques like micro-CT scanning, which allows researchers to see inside fossils without breaking them, the team behind the new work found many differences between Tomistoma and the Mokattam Formation crocs. Comparing measurements of the skull to those of modern and fossil gavials revealed that the roughly 18-inch-long noggin represented not just a new species, but a new genus as well.

They named it Herugavialis cairensis, drawing inspiration from the Egyptian god Heru, also known as Horus. Some Egyptian texts call the Sphinx “Horus of the Horizon.” The associations between the H. cairensis skull and the iconic Sphinx go beyond the material that yielded them. Both are missing the tips of their noses.
Did you know? The origin of the Sphinx’s name

The Egyptians did not refer to the great statue as the Sphinx. Rather, ancient Greeks started calling it that around 2,000 years after it was carved. They possibly did so because of its resemblance to their mythological sphinx, which had a lion’s body, a woman’s head and an eagle’s wings.

“We seek to connect Egypt’s deep natural history with its human history and the legacy of ancient Egyptian civilization,” study co-author Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University in Egypt, tells the Washington Post’s Elijah Wolfson. “Crocodiles were part of the Nile ecosystem, which was central to Egyptian life, and they held an important place in ancient Egyptian belief and culture.”

Gavials, cousins of crocodiles and alligators, were once found throughout the world. The Mediterranean region was home to a diverse community of crocodilians, including gavials, during much of the last 50 million years, lead author Paul Burke, a paleontologist at the Swedish Museum of Natural History, says in a statement. In fact, H. cairensis would have shared its shallow marine habitat with at least two other gavial species. Today, however, there are only two surviving gavials: the previously mentioned T. schlegelii and Gavialis gangeticus, which is clinging to habitats in Nepal and northern India.
Both are endangered, Burke tells Science News’ Jake Buehler. “So we should know about them and their long history.”

Correcting the fossil species’ identification also “helps paint a better picture of what large predators were like in the region,” Alex Hastings, a paleontologist at the Science Museum of Minnesota who did not participate in the study, tells CNN’s Taylor Nicioli. “This expands the known variety of forms of these amazing long-snouted crocodilians across the Mediterranean in ancient times.”
In ancient times, travelers journeying to Egypt via the Mediterranean Sea often faced perilous conditions.

As the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus wrote in the first century B.C.E., a sandbank extended along much of the kingdom’s northern coast, “not discernible to any who approach without previous experience of these waters.” Sailors who “in their ignorance turn with gladness toward the shore suffer unexpected shipwreck when their vessels suddenly run aground,” Diodorus added, “and now and then, mariners who cannot see land in time because the country lies so low are cast ashore before they realize it.” The only “safe harbor” to be found on this stretch of coastline, the historian concluded, was Pharos, the island that housed the Lighthouse of Alexandria.

Standing an estimated 330 to 430 feet tall, the lighthouse was also known as Pharos, after the land where it stood. At the time of its creation in the third century B.C.E., it was one of the world’s tallest humanmade structures, second only to the Pyramids of Giza. The lighthouse dominated the landscape for more than a millennium, until the 14th century C.E., when it crumbled into the sea following a series of earthquakes.

Some 700 years later, few traces of the lighthouse remain. But excavations on the neighboring island of Antirhodos, the site of an ancient palace that hosted the likes of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, have revealed a rare artifact linked to this lost wonder: a bronze signet ring depicting Pharos.

The ring is the “first of its kind known to exist,” the European Institute for Underwater Archaeology (IEASM) notes in a statement. Its design bears resemblance to portrayals of the lighthouse on Egyptian coins from the second century C.E. As archaeologist Isabelle Hairy writes for the Center for Alexandrian Studies, ancient currency offers “the most important documentary evidence” of Pharos’ appearance, suggesting that it had three tiers, including a square base, an octagonal middle section and a circular top. (Ancient writers left behind descriptions of the lighthouse, but these accounts are often conflicting, resulting in varying visual interpretations by later artists.)
Need to know: Wonders of the ancient world

- The structures most often cited as the seven wonders of the ancient world are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Colossus of Rhodes, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.
- Of these seven, only the Great Pyramid of Giza survives today.

Researchers from the institute recovered the ring as part of a joint archaeological mission with the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. According to a Facebook post shared by the ministry, archaeologists at the site have also found tableware, amphorae, oil lamps and fragments of glassware spanning the fourth century B.C.E. through the fourth century C.E.

“The discovery … is even more important, as [the ring] has been excavated in the legendary palace of the island of Antirhodos, that once upon a time was a center of power,” says Franck Goddio, IEASM’s founder and president, in the statement. The Greek geographer Strabo, who visited Alexandria in the first century B.C.E., described Antirhodos as “an isle lying off the artificial harbor, which has both a royal palace and a small harbor.” Its name, he added, was an allusion to its status as “a rival” of the Greek island of Rhodes.

For now, much about the ring remains unknown. “The statement does not say who wore this ring or what for,” Guillermo Carvajal writes for La Brújula Verde. “It gives neither its size nor its exact date.”

Still, the jewelry’s presence at the site has led the researchers to posit that the island once housed administrative offices designated for such tasks as management of the lighthouse. In ancient Egypt, bureaucrats used signet rings to sign legal documents; the pricey accessories also advertised their owners’ elite social status.

Construction of the lighthouse probably began during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who served as Egypt’s first Ptolemaic king, and wrapped up under his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who succeeded him upon his death in 282 B.C.E. The Greek architect Sostratus of Cnidos designed the revolutionary structure, which is often described as the world’s first recorded lighthouse.

Today, physical evidence of Pharos is limited largely to stone blocks and metal clamps used to bind these blocks together. “The architectural fragments lie scattered over 18 acres underwater,” Hairy told the New York Times’ Franz Lidz earlier this year. “The visibility is extremely bad, the seabed is uneven and there are no clear layers of sediment.”

These challenges haven’t stopped Hairy and her colleagues at the Pharos Project from embarking on a multidisciplinary effort to reconstruct the ancient wonder digitally, piecing together photogrammetry scans of the lighthouse’s sparse ruins to envision what it might have looked like in its heyday.

Although Hairy estimates that the work is “still generations from completion,” per the Times, the project’s findings are poised to transform historians’ understanding of the fabled lighthouse. Until then, those hoping to see Pharos for themselves need look no further than the newly discovered ring.

Throughout world wars, pandemics and the turn of centuries, there was Jonathan. As the world around him shifted and changed, he lived the slow life munching grass on Saint Helena, a British island territory some 1,200 miles off the western coast of Africa.

The Aldabra giant tortoise is the oldest turtle in recorded history and the world’s oldest living land animal. Caretakers don’t know his exact age, but a photograph from 1882 shows the tortoise looking fully grown, which, for his species, is at least 50 years old. This means that Jonathan would be about 194 today.
“To be honest, I suspect he’s older,” veterinarian Joe Hollins, who looks after Jonathan, told the Washington Post’s Cathy Free in 2022. “But we can never know.”

No matter Jonathan’s exact age, one thing seems certain: Something has made him exceptional when it comes to withstanding the test of time. He has already lived more than a century beyond his species’ 80-year average life expectancy—a feat that his safe environment, diet and medical care alone might not be able to explain.

In a new study published on Wednesday in Science Advances, researchers examined Jonathan’s DNA for genetic clues to his extraordinary age. To collect the data, Hollins propped Jonathan’s mouth open with a gloved finger and swabbed a sample of cheek cells and saliva.

“We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive,” says co-author Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies aging at the University of California, Los Angeles, to the New York Times’ Monique Brouillette.
Key context: False reports of Jonathan’s death

In April, false reports that Jonathan had died were circulated widely, stemming from a fake X post claiming to be the tortoise’s veterinarian. It turned out to be a hoax—a ploy for cryptocurrency donations.

The research team sequenced Jonathan’s DNA and identified 287 genetic variants that were unique to him. Many of these had to do with repairing damage to DNA, reducing inflammation and managing insulin. They also found that he shared aging-related genes with species including naked mole-rats, which almost never get cancer.

Additionally, they looked at Jonathan’s epigenome, the chemical tags on DNA that turn certain genes on and off. As organisms age, these switches become less predictable—tags might inconsistently attach or fall off, leading to erratic activity from genes. The team compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of four younger tortoises.

Overall, Jonathan showed the chaos, or entropy, in the epigenome that would be expected for his age. But in the areas of the genome linked to things like DNA repair and mitochondria, the energy-producing centers in cells, Jonathan’s chemical tags were especially youthful. At these spots, Jonathan’s epigenome looked similar to DNA from a 5-year-old juvenile tortoise that the researchers studied.

The work doesn’t prove that these markers are the reason for Jonathan’s long life, but they offer a clue to how DNA might endure for long periods. They also align with findings from supercentenarians, humans who have lived to be more than 110 years old.

“Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face,” study co-author Stephen Clark, founder and chief scientist at the nonprofit Kallel Foundation for aging research, says in a statement. “Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people.”

But before any of this information can find a medical use, scientists will have to conduct deeper research. For one, Jonathan’s cheek swab contained incomplete DNA, so the team combined his genome with a younger tortoise’s DNA, resulting in a code that was only about 95 percent Jonathan—and allowing for the possibility that some of his unique DNA variants were not included in the sample. A blood test would have produced a full genome, but because of the risk of infection for the tortoise, Saint Helena officials did not allow it.

What’s more, Jonathan is just one study subject, and it’s difficult to generalize any results based on a lone individual. His genome was also compared against only a small handful of other tortoises, as bioinformatics researcher Kousuke Hashimoto of the University of Osaka, Japan, tells New Scientist’s James Woodford, inviting the possibility that the other tortoises also had unique variants that were not identified. Nevertheless, he calls the study “fascinating.”

“The results integrate very well in the wider puzzle of what longevity is,” Björn Schumacher, who studies aging at the University of Cologne in Germany and was not involved in the study, tells the New York Times.

Jonathan was born in the Seychelles, an island nation in the Western Indian Ocean. But as a gift to the governor, he was brought to Saint Helena in 1882, when he was photographed as an adult. Since then, he has been living at Plantation House, the governor’s home, with other giant tortoises.

Hollins took charge of Jonathan’s care in 2009, when the animal was around 180 years old and not in great shape. Among markers of age, such as cataracts and a loss of smell that prevented him from finding his own food, the tortoise suffered from a soft beak that made it hard to graze. The veterinarian hand-fed Jonathan, who recovered and developed a razor-sharp edge to his beak within the next couple of years.
“He is symbolic of resilience, longevity, endurance,” Hollins tells Reuters’ Marta Serafinko, “a persistent presence throughout huge historic events.”
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- New York Jets running back Breece Hall and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell are ruled out for Week 5's game against the Cleveland Browns, coach Aaron Glenn told reporters Friday.
Glenn also said that left guard Dylan Parham and linebacker Kiko Mauigoa will not play Sunday.

Hall, who sustained a quadriceps injury in Week 3, would miss his second consecutive game. Mitchell missed the last two weeks due to a finger injury. Parham and Mauigoa are out with respective knee and quad injuries.

Second-string running back Braelon Allen started in place of Hall in the Jets' 23-12 loss to the Chicago Bears on Sunday in Chicago. He was in for 30 (94%) of the Jets' offensive snaps and totaled 67 yards from scrimmage off 16 touches. No other Jets running back logged a rushing attempt against the Bears.
Hall, who hasn't practiced since Week 3, totaled 265 yards from scrimmage and a score through his first three appearances this season.

Mitchell caught nine passes for 123 yards through his two appearances this season. The Jets started Garrett Wilson and Isaiah Williams at wide receiver over the last two weeks. Jordan Meredith filled in for Parham at left guard.

Glenn said defensive back Jarvis Brownlee, who is in the concussion protocol, is progressing well. Tight end Mason Taylor, who missed the last two games due to a thumb injury, is set to return in Week 5.
The Jets (1-3) will host the Browns (3-1) at 1 p.m. EDT Sunday in East Rutherford, N.J.
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- Hundreds of Marvel fans donned Spider-Man costumes at New York Comic Con in an attempt to break a Guinness World Record.

The Thursday event, organized by toy company Jazwares in collaboration with Disney Consumer Products, attempted to break the Guinness World Record for the largest gathering of people dressed as Spider-Man.
Organizers have not yet released an official count from the event, but acknowledged the final tally was just short of the current record of 685 participants.
The current record was set by Sony Pictures Entertainment Malaysia in 2023 to celebrate the theatrical release of Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.

Oct. 9 (UPI) -- President Donald Trump established a committee of inquiry Friday to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on allegations she made false statements in respect to "one or more mortgage instruments."

He announced the committee in a memorandum posted on the White House website. The committee comprises Kevin Hassett, Trump's adviser on economic policy; Keith Sonderling, labor secretary and acting director of the Office of Government Ethics; and Andrea Lucas, the chairman of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Trump's memo said that it's his job to fire "subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law." He said the committee would investigate and "report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal."

Trump first attempted to fire Cook from the Federal Reserve in 2025, accusing her of committing mortgage fraud in a loan application by incorrectly listing a property as a vacation home. The Supreme Court ruled against that effort in June, saying Trump needed proper justification.

In August, the Trump administration sent Cook a letter laying out its allegations and seeking a written response within 21 days. She said Trump has "no legal basis" to fire her and said the error on her mortgage loan application was an error.

"An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing," Cook's attorneys said in a statement. "These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will."
